newsitem.title: INDIA: Be patriotic like China businessmen, India PM says.
newsitem.headline: Be patriotic like China businessmen, India PM says.

text.p: Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda told Indian businessmen on Tuesday that they lacked the patriotism of their Chinese counterparts who had become key players in funding Beijing's economic reforms.
Deve Gowda told a meeting of the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI) that out of $20 billion recently invested in China, 80 percent had come from overseas Chinese.
"This cannot be said about Indians. Isn't this lack of patriotism?"
Departing from his prepared speech, Deve Gowda questioned the commitment of businessmen to the country's welfare since independence from Britain in 1947.

"How much Indian money has been siphoned out since independence?" he asked. "I am not going to blame the previous prime ministers, the finance (ministers) and the government alone. Let us collectively work together for the country."
India attracted $2 billion in foreign direct investment in the 1995/96 fiscal year ended on March 31. That was far below the $30 billion to $40 billion China has drawn in recent years.

Deve Gowda told FICCI's 69th annual meeting that he would consider the group's request to remove a recently introduced minimum alternate tax (MAT) on companies when the next year's budget is prepared.
But he said it would be unfair to blame the MAT, a minimum tax on companies which among other issues has been cited as the cause for a slide in the country's capital markets.
"Too much sensational statistics is being fed in to suggest an economic slowdown," Deve Gowda said. "It is true that certain sectors have to improve but others have done reasonably well."
Industrial production grew 8.6 percent April-August compared with the same period in 1995. That was far below the 12.6 percent growth rate in April-August 1995 over the same five months in 1994.

Responding to FICCI president Deepak Banker who said the economy was slowing because of a credit squeeze, Deve Gowda said his government was being unfairly accused of not doing enough to promote economic reforms.
Banker said business was suffering on account of an old law governing the country's foreign exchange regulations.

Deve Gowda said it was wrong to support businessmen if they were caught violating the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA). "When blatant violations of law have taken place, persons concerned cannot remain unpunished," he said.
Foreign businessmen claim FERA restrictions have been a major impediment to investments in India.
"Did you have stability in 1994-95 or not?" Deve Gowda asked, referring to a period of economic growth. "Was FERA there at that time or not?"
He said it was wrong to say his six-month-old minority alliance was responsible for industry's problems.
"We have been hearing that MAT, high interest rates and (political) uncertainty and confusion, speaking with different voices are responsible for a decline (in) the capital market.
"Day in and day out we are crying out. We are going for funds to the World Bank to the IMF (International Monetary Fund), as though there is no money in the country.
"I am not being emotional. I am a person who is concerned. Come to me after the parliament session. I will discuss your problems across the table."
